source_title: Mass protests challenge Macron as French police use tear gas and water cannons
source_excerpt:
PARIS — More than 100,000 people marched in Paris on Saturday over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging President Emmanuel Macron ’s government in a largely peaceful demonstration before clashes broke out near the march’s end point.
Paris police estimated turnout at 110,000, with demonstrators mobilizing despite restrictions that confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center.
Students, union members, environmentalists and other groups marched through cold, rainy weather. Near the march’s end point at Porte de Vincennes, some demonstrators threw bottles and rocks at police, who then charged at the crowd, fired tear gas and used water cannons. The clashes lasted about an hour. NBC News witnessed no looting.
Police used tear gas in several cities, including Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Marseille, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march’s end point.
The Paris prosecutor’s office said 64 people were arrested in connection with Saturday’s demonstration and 40 were placed in police custody. They included six minors. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.
The unrest is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: The far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for it.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had announced a nationwide deployment of up to 70,000 officers, backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
An Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d’Italie early in the afternoon. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.
At Porte de Vincennes, some demonstrators tried to continue toward Place de la Nation, but police blocked their path, French media reported.
Camille Chesnier, 27, said she had been unable to find work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats, and frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.

Another demonstrator, Domitille, 25, told NBC News that the people are protesting over several critical issues, including the cost of living.
“We are tired of the government because the cost of living is higher. The policeman just goes against the population — kids, everyone. ... And also fascists are rising in France. And we need to hear everyone, because we are tired and we need to be heard as citizens,” she said Saturday, noting it’s her first time protesting.
A small protest became a national movement
What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris has grown into a national movement. Students demanding better schools and workers seeking higher wages and pensions have brought anger over living standards into the final months of Macron’s presidency.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Police changed the Paris route Friday. On Saturday morning, police cleared Place de la Bastille, where protesters had originally been expected to gather. NBC News journalists were among those ordered out of the square and witnessed no resistance. Police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a 135-euro ($150) fine.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d’Italie.
“They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters,” she said. “But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools.”
A student studying cinema at Paris’ Sorbonne University told NBC News he joined the protests because of a police crackdown on demonstrations at Sorbonne Nouvelle University.
“They were, like, kicking people who were not involved in the protest inside the university, and it was a total mess,” he said.
“We are mostly students,” he added, referring to the protesters. “We’re not here to break things. We’re not here to mess with the cops or anyone. We’re just here to protest.”
In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier and other cities.
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orléans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretch of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
Nuñez acknowledged Monday that police lost control in some cities during last weekend’s unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.
More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday. About 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over the weekend.
Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34-year-old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
“I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”
Major museums, including the Louvre, the Orsay Museum, the Picasso Museum and the Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — were shuttered Saturday.
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
Public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours in the 2024-25 school year because absent teachers were not replaced, according to Education Ministry figures. That amounted to 7.5% of scheduled teaching time.
Students are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people,” said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University.
